I was dirt poor in college (late aughts). I paid around $400 rent (all bills split with a roommate), didn't heat (electric bill $20), no TV, no internet, and other utilities included in rent.

I couldn't afford junk food or fast food at all on my budget. Maybe once every couple of weeks something like that would be a treat. I normally ate frozen or canned veggies/fruit, beans, rice, and a bit of whatever fresh produce was on sale (if we could get $0.40 bell peppers, we'd stuff the beans and rice in there to be fancy). We spent around $75/person each month on food and it was fairly good for you.

Why do people say poor people can't afford to eat well? Is there some really cheap junk food I just never knew about? Are people finding a way to live on the dollar menu for less than $75/mo?

I see this claimed all the time and it's so incongruous with my experiences. It sounds as odd as if people claimed the poor couldn't afford to ride bikes places so they ended up stuck with crummy old cars.

You had the privilege of having access to a grocery store that is sheltered in a safe neighborhood. [And had good prices unlike Krogers or Foodland] If you lived in a food desert or didn't have transportation to a distant grocery store and the only thing within walking distance of your apartment complex was a McDonald's and a 7-11 you wouldn't have had such an easy time with it. You can afford junk food when it's the only food you get that day.

I don't get the comment on being able to afford junk if you don't eat everyday though. It seems like regardless of how often you eat it would be a better option to go for cheap stuff.

There is one thing to consider, portion sizes. When I was living alone it was difficult to grocery shop because any food that was broken down into individual portions was basically as expensive as fast food. Also, when your kitchen is a roast infested nightmare that has no chance of getting any better because your neighbors are trash and cleaning doesn't make the problem any better it really takes out your motivation to cook and bathe. (Who wants to get in a shower full of bugs?) I know I stopped using my fridge and sink because I couldn't make a meal with fighting a ton of bugs in the process. I have to study this subject matter as a course of making a living, and although you make some good points, I have to point out a few flaws in your thinking:

No. Planning is part of intelligence.

A) Intelligence is much more dynamic than that, although the ability to complete higher level planning is a sign of intelligence, it is not indicative of someones overall intellectual capacity. For instance, those who score higher on tests that measure creativity, tend to also show lower levels of long-term planning. Likewise, those who are more analytical straight-shooters are often better at planning, but also tend to be less creative. Both are highly intelligent, but they think, plan, and behave differently. It is compulsive behavior that defines them, and, strangely enough, often the one that coincides with poor planning (and creative intelligence).

B) The inability to follow through with said planning and the long-term ramifications is the bigger issue. What is often seen is that intelligent people with compulsive behavioral traits often start off early in life doing a lot of planning. Unfortunately as they learn that those plans never materialize, often with an awareness that they play a role in that, they stop planning long-term. It becomes a form of learned helplessness. Aggressive behavioral traits are also important here, as the inability to modulate behavior can be self-sabotaging.

Lack of motivation I'de say being far more dominating than compulsivity.

Studies show that lack of motivation is linked with the preoccupation of being in poverty. People in poverty tend to work longer, have less free time, are less financial security, and have larger families, all of which adds up to a saturation of attention and therefore reduced motivation to seek out alternatives. Basically, this is a way of saying that poverty can be self-perpetuating--in that because housing, food, and survival take precedence, creativity and education often take a back seat to life, even if they are aware that such things have the possibility of helping them climb out of poverty. The issue of food deserts is very real and common in US low income/poverty areas and regions.

Food deserts are real. Places where the only place to get anything to eat is convenience stores, which charge up to twice as much as what a grocery store would and usually don't have produce.

Riding a bike to a a store means owning a bike. In really poor areas you don't own things like bikes, because they'll just get stolen. Wasted money. Plus biking 10 miles to the nearest supermarket in 2 feet of snow isn't smart.

If you live somewhere like northern US, cheap produce is only 3-4 months of the year. Right now bell peppers on sale are $1.50 each. Potatoes are cheap. Pasta is cheap. Store brand cheese (not cheese slices, but cheese blocks) is cheap. Rice is cheap. That's the majority of what I lived on during the winter. Sometimes if there was a "manager's special" on a piece of meat, I might get that. "Manager's special" means "About to expire" - you have to cook it asap. My food budget was between $75-100/month when I it was bad.

No junk food, no fast food, no soda-pop, no pre-cooked food. Cheap coffee and tea bags and lots of water to drink. I was counting pennies to afford toothpaste and laundry soap. No tv. someone was paying for my (slow, but no complaints) internet. Used the car once a month to get groceries. (Bought it before I became poor.) "No heat" not an option in a place where it can go -10F at night in the winter. Sometimes someone would give me an amazon gift card. If you watch amazon carefully for sales you can sometimes get great deals on a case of non-perishable foods like pasta. Once I got a great deal on some discontinued packets of Indian food. It was a nice treat for a few meals.

For someone who almost became homeless 3 or 4 times I had it good. I had a car. I had a laptop (hand me down from a friend). I had internet paid by someone. I had pots from before I was poor. I wasn't starving. But i wasn't eating healthy. The doctors at the free clinic used to hand out bottles of multivitamins because malnutrition in poor people is so common.

For what it is worth, I'm in a better place now. I can afford those $1.50 peppers if I want one. I eat lots of fruits and vegetables. The habits from being really poor stick with you. No junk food outside of popcorn. No soda-pop. No fast food except for a monthly pizza. Can at least buy coffee that doesn't taste like brown crayon water. Can buy meat that's not about to expire but still go for sales. Still don't own a tv. and I can afford my own cheap internet now.

It's excuse making for poor decisions. I find it quite rich that the term "food desert" originated in the land that has vast amounts of food readily available. Generally, not adding dead weight to your family size, leaving the microwave alone and planning meals ahead all do wonders for keeping the food budget down (among other things), but some people are slaves to their own immediate desires. When you see the failure to pick up a 33 cent apple as opposed to a 95 cent pastry followed by cries of "inequality", you're gonna see a lot of other abject failure in other areas of life as well. It's less about how much money you have, and more about what you do with it. Impulsive, daft people make impulsive and daft decisions, no matter how much money is thrown at them to "equalize" things.
